SETUP01/65

MEAI 502 · CS 4082 · Fall 2026

Linear
Regression

Lecture 2 — The first learning algorithm, in full

Dr Naila Marir · Effat University · College of Engineering

Speaker notes

Last week was the map of the field. This week is the first algorithm, all the way down.

Open by setting expectations honestly: “Linear regression is the simplest useful model in machine learning. We are going to spend a whole lecture on it — and that is deliberate. Every idea you meet today comes back in every model for the rest of the semester: a hypothesis, parameters, a cost function, and an algorithm that minimises it. Learn the pattern here, where you can see all of it at once, and neural networks in Week 12 will be the same four boxes with more arithmetic.”

That framing matters. Students who think linear regression is "the easy one we rush past" do badly in Week 12.
SETUP02/65

Four ideas. Every model you will ever build.

A dataset. A model with parameters. A cost function that scores it. A learning algorithm that improves it. Today you see all four at once, on the simplest model there is.

Speaker notes

This is the thesis of the lecture, and it is worth saying slowly.

Tell them: “If you remember nothing else from today, remember these four boxes. When we get to logistic regression in Week 4, I will draw the same four boxes. SVMs in Week 9, same four boxes. Neural networks in Week 12, same four boxes — just a much bigger model and a harder optimisation.”

Then the honest caveat, because a sharp student will find it: unsupervised learning (Week 10) does not have a target y, so the cost function measures something else — distance to a cluster centre, reconstruction error. The shape survives; the contents change.

Speaker notes

Eight stops, in two halves. Say the shape out loud: “The first four build the model and the score. The last four are the algorithm that does the learning, and then what happens when you have more than one feature.”

Keep this quick — it is a signpost, not content. The numbering recurs on the section dividers, and the left rail jumps between them, so students always know where they are.

Point at 03 and 04 specifically: that is where students who only memorised the formula come unstuck in the midterm.
SETUP04/65

01

The four notions

  • Dataset
  • Model and its parameters
  • The cost function
  • The learning algorithm

Speaker notes

SETUP05/65

The four you must remember

01

Dataset

The examples you learn from. m pairs of (input, correct answer).

Today: house sizes and their prices

02

Model

A function with adjustable parameters. Changing them changes the predictions.

Today: a straight line, θ0 and θ1

03

Cost function

One number saying how wrong the current parameters are.

Today: mean squared error

04

Learning algorithm

The procedure that changes the parameters to make that number smaller.

Today: gradient descent

“Learning” is nothing more than notion 4 minimising notion 3 by adjusting notion 2 on notion 1.

Speaker notes

Spend real time on this slide — two or three minutes. It is the skeleton of the lecture and of the course.

Read the kick line at the bottom aloud, then say it again in plain words: “Learning is an algorithm turning knobs to make a number go down.” Students find that demystifying, and it is exactly true.

A question worth asking here: “Which of these four does the human choose, and which does the computer choose?” Answer: the human chooses 1, 2 and 3 — the data, the model family, and what counts as wrong. The computer only does 4. That is a point about responsibility, and it comes back when you talk about bias and about metric choice in Week 8.
SETUP06/65

The running example

A training set of house sizes and the prices they sold for.

We want to learn, from this data, how to predict the price of a house that is not in it.

Portland, Oregon. Size in square feet, price in thousands of dollars. This is the example that carries the whole lecture — every formula you meet today, you can point back at this picture.

Figure: Andrew Ng, Machine Learning (Stanford CS229 / Coursera), housing price dataset.

Speaker notes

Before showing any notation, get them to read the picture. Ask: “What do you see?” You want them to say, unprompted: bigger houses cost more, but not exactly — the points scatter.

Both halves matter. The trend is why a model is possible; the scatter is why the model will never be perfect, and why we will need a cost function to measure how imperfect.

Point at an outlier — the ~1450 sq ft house at 460k. Ask what might explain it. Waterfront, renovated, sold to family below market. Land the point: “Price is not a function of size. It is a function of size plus many things we did not measure. Our model will capture the part we did measure — and that is all any model ever does.”

Recall Lab 1 here: this is Stage 3, exactly the kind of scatter they made for the breast-cancer features.
SETUP07/65

This is supervised learning

We are given a dataset and we already know what the correct output should be for every example in it.
We assume a relationship exists between the input and the output — and we set out to find it.

And because the output is a continuous number — a price, not a category — this is a regression problem.

If the answer were “malignant / benign”, as in Lab 1, it would be classification. Same four notions, different model and different cost function. That is Week 4.

Speaker notes

Connect back to Lecture 1's taxonomy explicitly — draw the supervised/unsupervised split on the board again if it helps. Regression = continuous output. Classification = discrete output. That is the only distinction, and students should be able to classify a problem in one sentence by the end of this slide.

Quick cold call, three problems: predict tomorrow's electricity demand in Jeddah (regression); decide whether this transaction is fraud (classification); predict how many days a patient will stay in hospital (regression). The third one starts an argument — it is a count, not a truly continuous quantity — and that argument is worth two minutes. Real answer: people model it both ways, and the choice depends on the decision it feeds.
SETUP08/65

Notation

SymbolMeaning
mNumber of training examples — how many rows you have
x(i)The input variable of example i. Also called a feature.
y(i)The output, or target — the thing we are trying to predict
(x(i), y(i))One training example — a single row
{(x(i), y(i))} i = 1…mThe training set — the whole list of m examples
𝒳 , 𝒴The space of inputs and the space of outputs

The superscript is an index, not a power. x(2) is the second house, not x squared. The brackets are there precisely to remind you.

Speaker notes

Notation slides are boring to deliver and fatal to skip. Every single formula for the rest of the semester uses these symbols.

The one thing to say with emphasis is the last line: x(2) means the second training example. Students confuse it with a square at least once each year, usually in the middle of an exam. The parentheses are the convention that prevents it.

A second warning worth giving now: m is the number of examples; later today n will be the number of features. Different letters, different things, and they appear in the same formulas. Write both on the board and leave them there.

On 𝒳 and 𝒴: mention them, do not dwell. They matter when you talk about a model generalising to inputs it has not seen.
SETUP09/65

The same notation, on a real table

Size in feet²  (x)Price in $1000s  (y)
i = 12104460
i = 21416232
i = 31534315
i = 4852178
i = 53000540
⋮⋮⋮

(x(5), y(5)) = (3000, 540)  —  one training example: the fifth row.

The feature column is 𝒳. The output column is 𝒴. There are m rows in total, and m is a big number in any real dataset.

Speaker notes

Walk it physically. Put your finger on the highlighted row: “This row is one training example. Its x is 3000. Its y is 540. Together they are x superscript 5, y superscript 5.”

Then point down the first column — “this is what we're given” — and the second — “this is what we want to be able to produce when we are not given it.”

Ask them: what is x(3)? (1534.) What is y(2)? (232.) Three seconds each. This costs thirty seconds and saves a lot of confusion later.
SETUP10/65

Check yourself

Consider the training set below. (x(i), y(i)) is the i-th training example. What is y(3)?

  • A1416
  • B315
  • C1534
  • D0.1436
Answers on R B — 315. The third row, output column.

Speaker notes

Poll the room before revealing. Hands, or a quick Mentimeter.

The wrong answers are diagnostic, so read them out:
— C (1534) means they took the third row but the input column: they have the indexing right and the variable wrong.
— A (1416) means the second row, input column: off by one and in the wrong column. Ask whether they counted the header as a row.
— D is the nonsense option; nobody should pick it.

If more than a couple choose C, go back to slide 9 and re-do the finger-pointing. It is worth the minute — this notation is load-bearing for the next seventy slides.
MODEL11/65

02

The model

  • What a learning algorithm produces
  • The hypothesis h
  • Why a straight line

Speaker notes

MODEL12/65

How supervised learning works

Speaker notes

This diagram answers the question “what does a learning algorithm actually give you?” The answer is: a function. Not a number, not a report — a function you can call on new inputs.

Trace the flow with your hand, top to bottom then left to right. “Training set in. Algorithm runs — once, offline, maybe for hours. Out comes h. Then, forever after, a new house arrives, goes in the left of h, and an estimated price comes out the right.”

The point students miss: training and prediction are two different moments. Training is expensive and happens rarely; prediction is cheap and happens constantly. That asymmetry is the whole reason deployment (Stage 7 in the Lab 1 lifecycle) is its own engineering problem.

Historical aside, if there is time: h stands for hypothesis. It is a bad name — nobody is testing a hypothesis in the scientific sense — but it comes from the early literature and it stuck. Ng says the same thing in his lectures.
MODEL13/65

How do we represent h?

We have to choose a shape for h before we can learn anything. Look at the data and pick the simplest shape that could plausibly fit.

Hypothesis

hθ(x) = θ0 + θ1x

A straight line. This model is called linear regression with one variable, or univariate linear regression.

Speaker notes

This is the single most important conceptual move in the lecture, and it goes by fast unless you slow it down.

Say it explicitly: “Machine learning does not invent the model. We choose the family — here, straight lines — and the algorithm picks the best member of that family. Choosing the family is a human decision, and it is where most of your judgement as a practitioner goes.”

Anticipate the good question — “why a line? the data isn't exactly a line” — and answer it honestly, don't wave it away:
1. It is the simplest thing that captures the trend we can all see.
2. It has exactly two parameters, so we can visualise everything today. With twenty parameters you could not draw any of the pictures in this lecture.
3. It is often good enough, and when it is not, you will see it in the residuals.
4. Everything harder — polynomials, logistic regression, neural networks — is built by making this shape more flexible.

Notation note: θ is theta. θ0 and θ1 are the parameters, sometimes called weights or coefficients. Students will meet all three words; they mean the same thing. The subscript θ on h just reminds you that h depends on them — you will often see it written plain as h(x).
MODEL14/65

Two knobs, and what each one does

Speaker notes

Students have seen y = mx + c since school. Say that out loud — “this is the line equation you already know, with different letters” — because the unfamiliar θ notation makes some of them think it is new mathematics. It is not.

Give both parameters a meaning in the problem, which is the part school never did:
— θ1 is dollars per square foot. It is the interpretable one, and it is the number a client would actually ask about.
— θ0 is the predicted price of a house of zero square feet. Which is nonsense as a house, but the line needs somewhere to start. Say this plainly: “θ0 often has no physical meaning. It is there so the line does not have to pass through the origin.”

Worth asking: “What would it mean if θ1 came out negative?” Bigger houses are cheaper — which would make you go back and check your data, not your model. That instinct is exactly what you want them to develop.
MODEL15/65

Read the parameters off the line

Consider the plot of hθ(x) = θ0 + θ1x. What are θ0 and θ1?

  • Aθ0 = 0, θ1 = 1
  • Bθ0 = 0.5, θ1 = 1
  • Cθ0 = 1, θ1 = 0.5
  • Dθ0 = 1, θ1 = 1
Intercept: the line meets the y axis at 0.5 → θ0 = 0.5
Slope: from x = 0 to x = 2, y goes 0.5 → 2.5. Rise 2 over run 2 → θ1 = 1
Answer on RB

Speaker notes

Give them thirty seconds, then poll before revealing.

C is the trap, and it is the common wrong answer — it swaps the two parameters. If several students pick it, that tells you they can find both numbers but have not attached them to the right symbol. Fix it by going back to slide 14 and saying: θ0 is the one with no x next to it, so it is the one that does not change when x changes — the intercept.

Press R and walk the arithmetic out loud. Rise over run is the whole method, and it is worth doing once by hand so that when gradient descent later finds θ1 = 1 numerically, they know what the answer should be.
COST16/65

03

The cost function

  • What makes one line better than another
  • Squared error
  • The objective J(θ0, θ1)

Speaker notes

COST17/65

Which line?

Every choice of θ0 and θ1 gives a different line. There are infinitely many.

How do we come up with values of θ0 and θ1 that correspond to a good fit to the data?

“Looks about right” is not an algorithm. We need to turn good fit into a number — and then make that number as small as possible.

Speaker notes

This is the hinge of the lecture. Everything before it built the model; everything after it is about choosing the parameters.

Make them do the work first. Point at two of the lines and ask the room which is better. They will answer instantly and confidently. Then ask the real question: “How do you know? Give me a rule I could program.”

That second question is much harder, and letting them struggle with it for thirty seconds is what makes the cost function feel like a solution rather than a formula to memorise. Common student proposals, all worth hearing:
— “the line closest to the points” → closest how? measured which way?
— “the one with the most points on it” → a line through two points beats a line near all of them, which is clearly wrong
— “add up the distances” → good, this is nearly right, and the next slides are about getting it exactly right

Land it: “Machine learning's answer is always the same. Define a number that measures wrongness, then minimise it.”
COST18/65

The idea

Choose θ0, θ1 so that hθ(x) is close to y
for our training examples (x, y).

Three words there still need defining:

close

Measure a gap how?

Vertically: hθ(x(i)) − y(i)

for all

Combine m gaps?

Add them, then divide by m

so that

Then what?

Minimise it

Speaker notes

This slide is deliberately an unpacking exercise. The sentence in the box is what you want; the three cards are the engineering it takes to make it precise.

On “close”: ask why we measure the gap vertically rather than perpendicular to the line. The answer is that we are predicting y from x, so the error we care about is the error in y — how many dollars we were off by. (Perpendicular distance gives you a different, also useful method — total least squares — which is not what regression does. Mention only if asked.)

On dividing by m: without it, a model on 10,000 houses would look far worse than the same model on 100 houses, purely because there were more terms in the sum. Dividing makes the cost comparable across datasets.

Do not give the formula yet. The next three slides build it one piece at a time, and the build is the teaching.
COST19/65

One example's error

Speaker notes

One point, one gap. Get this single quantity solid before summing anything.

Say the subtraction in the right order and insist on it: prediction minus actual. Students often write it the other way round. For the squared cost it happens not to matter — squaring kills the sign — but in the gradient it matters a great deal, and a sign error there sends gradient descent uphill. Establish the convention now.

Name it: this quantity is the residual. They will see the word in every statistics text and in scikit-learn's documentation, and residual plots are a standard diagnostic they will meet in the lab.

Ask: “This point sits above the line, so the error is negative. If another point sits below, its error is positive. What happens if I just add all the errors together?” Let them get there: they cancel. A terrible line with huge errors in both directions could total zero. That is the motivation for the next slide.
COST20/65

Why squared error?

If we summed…What goes wrong
the errorsPositive and negative errors cancel. A dreadful line can score zero. Useless.
the absolute errorsGenuinely usable — this is mean absolute error, MAE. But |·| has a corner at zero, so it is not differentiable there, and our algorithm will need derivatives.
the squared errorsSigns disappear, the function is smooth everywhere, big mistakes are punished more than small ones, and — as we will see — the surface it makes has exactly one minimum.

The squared error cost is the standard choice for regression. It is not the only one, and it is not always the right one.

Speaker notes

Do not present squaring as arbitrary or as "the formula". Every row of this table is a real reason.

The "big mistakes punished more" point deserves a number. Being off by 10 costs 100; being off by 20 costs 400 — four times as much for twice the error. Ask whether that is what they want. For house prices, arguably yes: one catastrophic estimate is worse than several small ones. But it also means squared error is sensitive to outliers, and a single badly-recorded house can drag the whole line. MAE is more robust for exactly that reason. This trade-off is real, and it comes back in the lab.

On differentiability: keep it brief here, but flag it forward — “in twenty slides we will need the slope of this function at every point, and |x| does not have one at zero.”

Honest framing to state plainly: “Squared error is the default, not the truth. Choosing a loss is Stage 1 work — it encodes what you think a mistake costs.”
COST21/65

Building J, one piece at a time

one example

( hθ(x(i)) − y(i) )2

sum over all m

m∑i=1 ( hθ(x(i)) − y(i) )2

average — the ½ is for later convenience

J(θ0, θ1) = 12m m∑i=1 ( hθ(x(i)) − y(i) )2

Speaker notes

Build it live, one box at a time, saying each step in words before the symbols appear. Students who watch a formula get assembled remember it; students handed the finished formula memorise it and forget it by the midterm.

Everyone asks about the 2. Answer it now rather than letting it nag: dividing by 2m instead of m makes the derivative come out clean, because differentiating the square brings down a factor of 2 that cancels it. It is pure convenience. “It does not change where the minimum is — only the height of the surface — and we only care about where.” That last sentence is the one to repeat: multiplying a cost function by any positive constant leaves the minimising θ unchanged.

Name the parts: this is the mean squared error, MSE. J is called the cost function or the objective function.

The crucial reading of this formula, worth stating twice: J is a function of θ, not of x. The data is fixed — it is sitting in the table and will never change. The θ are the variables. This is the mental flip that slide 25 onwards is entirely about, and it is the hardest idea in the lecture.
COST22/65

The objective, stated once and for all

minθ0, θ1  12m m∑i=1 ( hθ(x(i)) − y(i) )2

Read it aloud: “find the θ0 and θ1 that make the average squared error as small as possible.”

That is the entire problem of linear regression. Everything left in this lecture is how to solve it.

Speaker notes

Pause here. This is the summit of the first half.

Make the whole room read the formula aloud in English. It sounds like a gimmick and it works — students who can narrate a formula can manipulate it; students who only recognise its shape cannot.

Point at the min and its subscript and say what they do: “the subscript tells you which quantities you are allowed to vary. We vary θ0 and θ1. We do not vary x or y — those are given to us.”

Then set up the rest of the lecture: “We now have a precise mathematical question. The remaining problem is that there are infinitely many pairs (θ0, θ1) and we cannot try them all. Section 5 is an algorithm that finds the answer without trying them all.”
COST23/65

Loss function vs cost function

Loss measures the error on one training example.

( hθ(x(i)) − y(i) )2
Cost is the average of the loss over the whole training set.

J(θ) = 12mm∑i=1 lossi

Both measure how far predictions are from reality. In practice the two words are used loosely and often interchangeably — including in the scikit-learn documentation — so read from context rather than assuming.

Speaker notes

A short, useful distinction. Make it once, then be relaxed about it — because the field is.

Why it is worth knowing at all: the distinction becomes operationally important in Week 12. Stochastic gradient descent updates parameters using the loss on one example (or a small batch) at a time rather than the cost over everything, and that is the difference between training a neural network in hours and not being able to train it at all.

If a student asks about "objective function": it is the more general word for whatever you are optimising — which may include a regularisation term that is not an error at all. They will meet that in Week 8.
INTUITION24/65

04

What does J look like?

  • Simplify to one parameter
  • Plot J against θ1
  • Then two parameters: bowls and contours

Speaker notes

Announce the strategy before you start, because it is a teaching device and students should know it is one: “We are going to make the problem artificially simpler — one parameter instead of two — so that we can draw a picture of it. Then we will put the second parameter back.”

Simplify, visualise, generalise. It is how good applied mathematics is done, and naming the move helps them do it themselves later.
INTUITION25/65

Simplify: drop θ0

The real problem

Hypothesis
hθ(x) = θ0 + θ1x
Parameters
θ0, θ1
Cost
J(θ0,θ1) = 12mm∑i=1(hθ(x(i))−y(i))2
Goal
minθ0,θ1 J(θ0, θ1)

Simplified — for today's pictures

Hypothesis
hθ(x) = θ1x
Parameters
θ1
Cost
J(θ1) = 12mm∑i=1(hθ(x(i))−y(i))2
Goal
minθ1 J(θ1)

Setting θ0 = 0 forces the line through the origin. One parameter left — so J can be drawn as an ordinary curve.

Speaker notes

Show the two frames side by side and name exactly what changed: θ0 is gone, so the line must pass through the origin. It can only pivot, not slide.

Be clear this is temporary and for drawing purposes only — “we put θ0 back in eight slides” — so nobody writes down the simplified version as the real model.

The four-row frame itself is the thing to notice. Say so: “Hypothesis, parameters, cost, goal. Every supervised learning method in this course fits in this box. When you meet a new algorithm, fill in these four rows and you understand it.” You will reuse this exact frame for multivariate regression at slide 57, and it is worth putting on the board for logistic regression in Week 4 too.
INTUITION26/65

Two plots that are easy to confuse

Same letters, completely different pictures. The left plot lives in data space. The right plot lives in parameter space.

Speaker notes

This is the hardest slide in the lecture and the one that pays off most. Do not rush it. If students leave today understanding only this distinction, the lecture succeeded.

Say it three ways:
1. Left: I have picked a line, here is how it sits against the data.
2. Right: here is how good each possible line is, as I sweep the knob.
3. Every single point on the right-hand plot corresponds to an entire left-hand picture.

That third sentence is the key, and it is worth writing on the board. One dot in parameter space = one whole line in data space.

An analogy that lands well: the left plot is a photograph of one candidate; the right plot is the scoreboard for every candidate. You look at the scoreboard to choose, then look at the photograph to see what you chose.

Warn them the axes are about to change meaning between consecutive slides and that this is intentional. Students who do not notice the switch get lost for the next six slides.
INTUITION27/65

Try θ1 = 1

The data: (1,1), (2,2), (3,3). With θ1 = 1 the line passes exactly through every point.

J(1) = 12·3 [ 02 + 02 + 02 ] = 0

Zero cost. A perfect fit — which happens only with invented data, never with real houses.

Speaker notes

Do the arithmetic out loud, slowly, all three terms. It takes fifteen seconds and it makes J concrete rather than symbolic.

h(1) = 1, and y = 1, so the error is 0. Same for the other two. Sum of squares 0, divided by anything, is 0.

Say clearly that this data is artificial. Real data never gives J = 0, and if it ever does, you have a bug or you are fitting noise — a thought to plant now that you will harvest when you teach overfitting in Week 8.

Now set up the sweep: “One value of θ1, one value of J. Plot that as a single dot at (1, 0) on the right-hand axes. Now let's do it again with a different θ1.”
INTUITION28/65

Try θ1 = 0.5

J(0.5) = 16 [ (0.5−1)2 + (1−2)2 + (1.5−3)2 ] = 0.25 + 1 + 2.256 ≈ 0.58

Speaker notes

Work the three predictions on the board: h(1) = 0.5, h(2) = 1, h(3) = 1.5. Against the true values 1, 2, 3, so the errors are −0.5, −1, −1.5.

Note the errors are all negative — the line under-predicts everywhere — and that squaring makes this invisible to the cost. Worth a passing remark: a systematically biased model and a noisy model can have the same MSE. That is a limitation of the metric, and it is why residual plots exist.

Then plot the second dot: (0.5, 0.58). Two dots now. Ask what they expect the shape of the curve to be. Some will already say "a parabola" — good, but make them justify it: the cost is a sum of squares of things that are linear in θ1, so it is quadratic in θ1. That is a genuine derivation, not a guess.
INTUITION29/65

Try θ1 = 0

J(0) = 16 [ 12 + 22 + 32 ] = 146 ≈ 2.33

Three points on the curve so far: (0, 2.33) · (0.5, 0.58) · (1, 0). Keep sweeping θ1 and the shape appears.

Speaker notes

θ1 = 0 gives the flat line h(x) = 0 — it predicts zero for every house, regardless of size.

This is a useful model to name: it is the worst sensible baseline, and it connects directly to the DummyClassifier they used in Lab 1 part 2. In regression the equivalent dummy predicts the mean of y. Remind them: “every real model gets compared to a baseline, or its score means nothing.”

Now you have three dots. Ask them to sketch the curve through them in their notes before you show the next slide. Making a prediction, then seeing it confirmed, is worth far more than being shown the answer.
INTUITION30/65

Compute one yourself

A training set with m = 3, plotted at right. The hypothesis is hθ(x) = θ1x and the cost is J(θ1) = 12mm∑i=1(hθ(x(i))−y(i))2.  What is J(0)?

  • A0
  • B1/6
  • C1
  • D14/6 ≈ 2.33
θ1 = 0 → every prediction is 0
errors: 0−1 = −1 · 0−2 = −2 · 0−3 = −3
squares: 1 + 4 + 9 = 14
J = 14 / (2 × 3) = 14/6 ≈ 2.33
Answer and working on RD — 14/6 ≈ 2.33

Speaker notes

Give them ninety seconds and make them actually compute it, on paper, individually. This is the first time they use the cost function as a tool rather than watch it being used. Do not let it become a demonstration.

Walk the room while they work — you will see immediately who has understood.

The distractors diagnose specific errors:
— C (1): divided by 2m = 6 but summed the errors instead of the squares, or forgot to square the 3.
— B (1/6): squared only one term.
— A (0): confused this with θ1 = 1 from slide 27 — a reading error, not a maths error, and worth pointing out gently.

Press R to show the full working, then ask a follow-up that costs nothing and teaches a lot: “Without computing it — is J(2) bigger or smaller than J(0)?” (Bigger: predictions 2, 4, 6 against 1, 2, 3 gives squared errors 1 + 4 + 9 = 14, identical by symmetry. A nice surprise, and it hints that the parabola is centred at θ1 = 1.)
INTUITION31/65

Sweep θ1 and the shape appears

A parabola, with its lowest point at θ1 = 1.

Our objective is the best possible line. So we minimise J — and here, θ1 = 1 is the global minimum.

Which is exactly the line we drew on slide 27. The picture and the arithmetic agree.

Speaker notes

The payoff of the last four slides. Let it land.

Say why the shape matters, not just what it is. A parabola has one lowest point, no other dips, and it slopes toward that point from every direction. So an algorithm that simply "walks downhill" cannot get stuck anywhere else — it must arrive at the answer. That is the promise gradient descent will cash in section 05, and it is the reason we get to make that promise at all.

Define global minimum properly here — the lowest point of the entire function, as opposed to a local minimum, which is merely lower than everything nearby. Slides 51 and 62 both turn on the difference.

The obvious student question, which you should invite: “If we can just draw the curve and look, why do we need an algorithm?” Excellent question. Answer: because with two parameters you need a 3-D surface, and with the thirty features from Lab 1 you would need a thirty-dimensional surface that nobody can draw or scan. Grid search dies of dimensionality almost immediately. “The picture is a teaching aid. The algorithm is what actually scales.”

Now put θ0 back

Two parameters, so J is a surface over the θ0–θ1 plane. The parabola became a bowl.

Speaker notes

Make the dimension bookkeeping explicit, because it is where students silently lose track:
— 1 parameter → J is a curve in 2-D (θ1 across, J up)
— 2 parameters → J is a surface in 3-D (θ0 and θ1 on the floor, J up)
— n parameters → a surface in n+1 dimensions, which nobody can picture

The floor is parameter space; the height is the cost. Say that sentence and then repeat it, because every diagram for the rest of the lecture uses it.

Then the honest limit: “This is the last picture of this kind you will ever get. Lab 1's dataset had thirty features, so its cost surface lives in thirty-one dimensions. We keep the intuition — downhill is downhill — and we give up the picture.”

A physical analogy that works: the bowl is a landscape and you are standing on it in fog. You cannot see the bottom, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. That is precisely the information gradient descent uses.

Left: one particular (θ0, θ1) drawn as a line through the data. Right: that same choice, drawn as a single dot in parameter space.

If any students have hiked or read a topographic map, ask them to explain contour lines to the room — it takes ten seconds and lands better from a peer.

Then connect the two panels explicitly, because this is slide 26's idea returning in its final form. Note the elongated, tilted ellipses. That shape is not decoration: it means the cost is far more sensitive to one parameter than the other, which makes gradient descent zig-zag and converge slowly. This is exactly the problem that feature scaling fixes — the StandardScaler from Lab 1 part 2. Say that connection out loud; students who met scaling as an arbitrary ritual finally see the reason for it here.

Speaker notes

Tell them what they are about to learn and why it is disproportionately important: “Gradient descent is not a linear regression technique. It is the optimisation algorithm behind almost all of modern machine learning. DESCENT35/65

The idea

Gradient descent is an iterative, first-order optimisation algorithm for finding a minimum of a function.

the recipe

  • Start at some θ0, θ1 — anywhere
  • Look at which way is downhill
  • Take a small step that way
  • Repeat until you stop going down

Iterative — it improves a guess repeatedly rather than solving in one shot. First-order — it uses only the slope (first derivative), not the curvature.

Speaker notes

The fog analogy is the one to use, and it should be vivid. You are on a hillside in thick fog. You cannot see the valley. But you can feel the slope beneath your feet. So you take a step in the steepest downhill direction, stop, feel again, step again. Eventually the ground is flat and you have arrived.

The two properties in the note are worth unpacking briefly:
— Iterative: unlike solving a quadratic with a formula, you approach the answer rather than landing on it. You must decide when to stop.
— First-order: it only feels the slope. Second-order methods (Newton's) also feel the curvature and converge in fewer steps, but each step costs far more. For large models, cheap steps win.

The one honest caveat, and it matters: gradient descent finds a minimum, not necessarily the minimum. On a bumpy landscape you end up in whichever valley you started above. Slide 47 shows this, and slide 49 explains why linear regression is spared the problem.
DESCENT36/65

Problem setup

Have
some function J(θ0, θ1)
Want
minθ0, θ1 J(θ0, θ1)

outline of the algorithm

Start with some θ0, θ1
Keep changing them to reduce J
until we hopefully end up at a minimum

Note the word hopefully. It is doing real work, and slides 38 and 43 explain what can go wrong.

Speaker notes

Point at “hopefully” and say you chose it deliberately. Two things can go wrong, and both are coming up: the step size can be wrong (too small and you wait forever, too large and you fly off), and the landscape can have several valleys.

Also worth saying: “notice this setup never mentions linear regression.” Gradient descent minimises any differentiable function. We will point it at our cost function in section 06, but the algorithm does not know or care where J came from. That generality is exactly why it matters so much.
DESCENT37/65

Walking down the surface

Start somewhere. Step downhill. Repeat. Start somewhere else, and you may land somewhere else.

Speaker notes

Trace one path with your finger, step by step, and narrate: “here, the ground slopes that way, so we step that way. Now here, it slopes this way…”

Then trace the second path from the other starting point and let the room notice, for themselves, that it ends somewhere different.

This is a genuinely surprising property and students should feel that. The algorithm is entirely deterministic, yet the answer depends on where you began — because it only ever knows the ground immediately underfoot. It has no map.

This is a real limitation of gradient descent on general problems and a live issue in deep learning, where random initialisation is a design decision with real consequences. Flag Week 12.

Then reassure, and make them wait for it: “For linear regression specifically, this cannot happen. The reason is on slide 49.”
DESCENT38/65

The gradient descent algorithm

repeat until convergence {

θj := θj − α ∂∂θj J(θ0, θ1)

(for j = 0 and j = 1)

}

:=

Assignment

“Becomes”. Not an equation to solve — an instruction to overwrite the old value.

α

Learning rate

How big a step to take. You choose it; the algorithm does not.

∂J/∂θj

Partial derivative

The slope of J in the θj direction — which way is uphill, and how steeply.

Speaker notes

The central formula of the lecture. Give it three or four minutes and take the three symbols one at a time.

:= versus = — worth being fussy about. a := a + 1 is a sensible instruction; a = a + 1 is a false statement. Programmers get this instantly; it is the difference between = and == in Python.

The minus sign is the whole algorithm. The derivative points uphill. We want to go down. So we subtract. Ask them what would happen with a plus sign — the cost would increase every step and run away to infinity. This is a real bug people write, and it announces itself loudly.

Why the derivative is the perfect quantity here: its sign tells you which way to go, and its magnitude tells you how far you are from flat ground. So the steps are large when you are far from the minimum and automatically shrink as you approach. The algorithm slows down near the answer without being told to. Say that explicitly — students find it elegant, and it explains why a fixed α still converges.

On partial derivatives: if their calculus is shaky, define it in one sentence — “the slope of J if you move θ1 and hold θ0 frozen” — and reassure them that in section 06 you hand them the result, already differentiated. They need to read it, not derive it.
DESCENT39/65

The learning rate α

α is a tuning parameter that sets the step size at each iteration.

You do not learn α from the data. You choose it — which makes it a hyperparameter, not a parameter.

θ0 and θ1 are parameters: the algorithm finds them. α is a hyperparameter: you set it before training starts, and if you set it badly, training fails.

Speaker notes

Introduce the word “hyperparameter” properly here — it is one of the most useful pieces of vocabulary in the course and it recurs constantly.

The distinction, stated crisply: parameters are learned from data; hyperparameters are chosen by you before learning starts. θ is learned. α is chosen. k in k-nearest-neighbours (Week 5) is chosen. The number of layers in a network (Week 12) is chosen.

Then the natural follow-up question, which you should raise yourself: “How do you choose it well?” Honest answer: you try several and see which works — but you must not judge them on the test set, or you have leaked. That is what a validation set is for, and it is Week 8. Plant it now.

Typical values in practice: 0.001 to 0.3. A common approach is to try 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1 and look at how the cost falls over iterations. Which is exactly what they will do in the lab.
DESCENT40/65

Too small, too large

α too small
Tiny steps. It still converges — but it can take an unreasonable number of iterations to get there.
α too large
It overshoots the minimum, can bounce further out each time, and may diverge — the cost grows instead of shrinking.

Speaker notes

Both panels use the same function and the same starting point. The only difference is a step coefficient of 0.005 against 0.05 — a factor of ten in α turns convergence into divergence. Say that number out loud; it makes the sensitivity concrete.

The practical diagnostic they must take away: plot J against iteration number, every time you train. If the curve goes down and flattens, you are fine. If it goes up, or oscillates wildly, α is too big — reduce it by a factor of ten and run again. If it goes down but is still falling steeply when you run out of iterations, α is too small or you need more iterations.

That plot is a required deliverable in the lab. Tell them so now.

A subtlety worth a sentence if the group is strong: too-large α does not always diverge. It can also oscillate around the minimum without ever settling. “Diverge” is the dramatic failure; “never quite settles” is the common one.
DESCENT41/65

Update both at once

A subtle bug that will not crash. It just quietly computes a different algorithm — one that may still converge, so you may never notice.

Speaker notes

This slide is here because it is the classic implementation bug, and because it is invisible. There is no error message. The code runs. The cost often still goes down. It is simply no longer gradient descent.

Walk the right-hand panel line by line so they see the mechanism: θ0 is assigned on line 2; when line 3 computes temp1, the partial derivative is evaluated at the new θ0, not the old one. The two parameters are meant to step from the same point.

The physical intuition: the gradient describes the slope at the point you are standing on. Both coordinates must step from that point. Moving one foot, then re-measuring the slope for the other, means you are no longer following the gradient you computed.

The NumPy connection, which is the useful takeaway for the lab: if you hold θ as a vector and write theta = theta - alpha * grad, you get simultaneous update for free, because the whole right-hand side is evaluated before any assignment happens. Writing it element by element in a Python loop is what invites the bug. Vectorise, and the problem disappears.
DESCENT42/65

Why the minus sign is all you need

From either side the step goes toward the minimum — and the algorithm was never told which side it was on.

Speaker notes

Take the two cases one at a time, and ask the room to predict each before you reveal it.

Left panel — starting on the right. Trace the amber tangent with your hand: it rises to the right, so the derivative is a positive number. Now substitute out loud, slowly: θ1 minus α (positive) times a positive number. Positive times positive is positive. Subtracting a positive makes θ1 smaller. Smaller θ1 means moving left along the axis. Left is toward the minimum. Correct.

Right panel — starting on the left. The mirror case. The violet tangent falls to the right, so the derivative is negative. Say the key step plainly, because this is where a few students stumble: “minus a negative is plus.” So θ1 increases, which moves right, which is again toward the minimum.

Then close the argument with the sentence that makes it click: “From the right it moves left. From the left it moves right. In both cases, toward the minimum — and the algorithm never knew which side it was on. The minus sign does all of it.”

That is the elegance of gradient descent in one line. Students who follow this argument never mis-remember the update rule, because they can re-derive it from the picture rather than recalling it.

Note the green arrows are the step, not the gradient. The gradient points uphill in both panels; we move the other way. If a sharp student asks why the arrows are shorter near the bottom, that is the next idea: the gradient shrinks as you approach, so the steps shrink too.
DESCENT43/65

What if you are already there?

Suppose θ1 is already at a local optimum of J(θ1), as shown. What will one step of gradient descent do?

  • ALeave θ1 unchanged
  • BChange θ1 in a random direction
  • CMove θ1 toward the global minimum of J
  • DDecrease θ1
At a minimum the tangent is flat, so the derivative is 0.
θ1 := θ1 − α·0 = θ1   — the update does nothing.
Answer on RA — it stays put.

Speaker notes

Poll first. Most get it, and the reasoning is what matters: flat tangent → derivative 0 → the update term vanishes → θ does not move.

Option C is the interesting distractor and deserves discussion even if nobody picks it. Ask: “why can't it move toward the global minimum?” Because gradient descent has no idea the global minimum exists. It knows only the slope where it is standing, and that slope is zero. It is stuck — permanently. This is the fog analogy paying off: you have reached flat ground, so you stop, even if a deeper valley lies over the ridge.

Two things follow, both worth saying:
1. This is how the algorithm terminates — it converges because the steps shrink to nothing.
2. This is also how it fails on non-convex problems, and it is exactly why slide 49 matters.
DESCENT44/65

“Repeat until convergence” — but when do you stop?

Stopping ruleIn practice
Cost stops improvingStop when J changes by less than some small ε between iterations. The most principled rule, and the usual default.
Fixed iteration budgetRun 1,000 iterations and stop. Crude, but predictable — and what you will do in the lab.
Gradient near zeroStop when the slope is essentially flat. Equivalent to the first rule in most cases.
Validation score worsensEarly stopping. Not about optimisation at all — it is about generalisation. Week 8.

Gradient descent approaches the minimum but never exactly reaches it. “Converged” always means “close enough”, and you decide what close enough is.

Speaker notes

The original slides say “repeat until convergence” and leave it there. This slide is the addition that makes it implementable — the difference between reading the algorithm and writing it.

The closing note is the important one: gradient descent is asymptotic. The steps get smaller as the gradient shrinks, so you creep toward the minimum forever without landing on it. Every practical implementation therefore needs a stopping rule, and that rule is a choice.

In the lab they will use the fixed budget with a cost-versus-iteration plot, because seeing the curve flatten teaches more than a tolerance check that silently returns.

The last row is deliberately a forward reference — flag it as a different kind of thing. Early stopping asks not “have I optimised enough?” but “have I optimised too much?”, which will not make full sense until overfitting in Week 8.

TOGETHER46/65

Two things we built separately

The algorithm on the left will minimise any differentiable function. The function on the right is the one we want minimised. Substitute.

Speaker notes

Hold the two halves up side by side and let them sit for a moment before moving.

Make the general point, because it is the one that transfers: “This is how machine learning is assembled. A model, a cost function, and an optimiser — three independent pieces, designed separately, snapped together. Swap the model for logistic regression and keep the optimiser. Swap the cost for cross-entropy and keep the optimiser. In Week 12 we swap in a neural network with millions of parameters, and the optimiser is still recognisably this.”

That modularity is not an accident of exposition — it is how the libraries are actually built. In scikit-learn, in PyTorch, the model and the optimiser really are separate objects that you compose.

All that remains is to compute the derivative of that particular J. That is the next slide.
TOGETHER47/65

Working out the derivative

the cost

J(θ0, θ1) = 12m m∑i=1 ( θ0 + θ1x(i) − y(i) )2

j = 0

∂J∂θ0 = 1m m∑i=1 ( hθ(x(i)) − y(i) )

j = 1

∂J∂θ1 = 1m m∑i=1 ( hθ(x(i)) − y(i) ) · x(i)

Chain rule. The square brings down a 2, which cancels the 2 in 2m — that is what the ½ was for. The only difference between the two is the trailing x(i), which is the derivative of the inside with respect to θ1.

Speaker notes

Decide in advance how much calculus this group wants. For a graduate class, derive the θ1 case on the board — it takes two minutes and is genuinely straightforward chain rule. For a mixed group, show the result and explain the structure.

Either way, point out the three things that make the result readable:
1. The 2 cancels. Here is the payoff for the ½ you promised on slide 21. Circle back to it explicitly — students appreciate a loose end being tied.
2. Both start the same way — the average error. That common factor is the "how wrong are we, on average" signal.
3. θ1's version is weighted by x(i). This is worth interpreting, not just stating: examples with large x pull harder on the slope. A big house that is badly predicted moves θ1 more than a small house that is equally badly predicted — which is right, because the slope has more leverage out there.

Point 3 is also the deep reason feature scaling matters. If one feature is measured in thousands and another in fractions, their gradients differ by orders of magnitude, so one parameter races while the other crawls. That is the elongated contour from slide 33, and it is why StandardScaler was not an arbitrary ritual in Lab 1 part 2.
TOGETHER48/65

Gradient descent for linear regression

This is the complete algorithm. Nothing is left undefined — every symbol here is either your data, your chosen α, or a number you already have.

Update θ0 and θ1 simultaneously, as on slide 41. In code: compute both, then assign both.

Speaker notes

The destination of the whole lecture. Say so: “Everything we have done today was to be able to write these four lines. You can implement this. You will, this week.”

Walk one iteration out loud so it is procedural rather than symbolic:
1. With the current θ, predict every house → m numbers
2. Subtract the true price from each → m errors
3. Average them → that is the θ0 gradient
4. Multiply each error by its x, then average → that is the θ1 gradient
5. Step both θ down by α times their gradient
6. Go to 1

Name it: this is batch gradient descent — "batch" because every step uses all m examples. With a million rows, each step reads the whole million. That is the motivation for stochastic and mini-batch variants, which is a Week 12 topic; mention the name now so it is not new later.

Ask a cost question if there is time: how much work is one iteration? O(m) per parameter. Cheap per step, many steps — which is the trade gradient descent always makes.
TOGETHER49/65

Why linear regression is lucky

The squared-error cost of a linear model is always a convex function — a single bowl.

One minimum. No local traps. Gradient descent will always find the global optimum, wherever you start it.

This is a mathematical guarantee about this specific combination of model and cost, not a general property of gradient descent.

Speaker notes

Here is the promise made on slide 37, kept.

Define convex informally but precisely enough to be useful: pick any two points on the surface, join them with a straight line, and the line never dips below the surface. One consequence is the one that matters here — a convex function has exactly one minimum, and any local minimum is the global minimum.

Then be clear about scope, because students over-generalise this: convexity here is a property of squared error applied to a linear model. Change either ingredient and it can vanish. Logistic regression with cross-entropy happens to stay convex (Week 4). A neural network is emphatically not convex (Week 12) — its cost surface is the bumpy one from slide 37, full of local minima and saddle points.

The intellectually honest punchline, which is worth saying: deep learning works anyway. In very high dimensions, most flat points are saddles rather than bad minima, and the minima you do reach tend to be good enough. That was a genuine surprise to the field, and it is not fully explained even now. Students enjoy hearing that there are open questions this close to the material.
TOGETHER50/65

Watch it learn

Left: the line moving through data space. Right: the same run as a dot sliding down the bowl in parameter space. One run, two views.

Speaker notes

Slide 27's distinction, now animated and joined. This is the payoff, and it is worth narrating carefully.

Say which panel to watch and when. Early on, the dot is high on the wall of the bowl and the line is visibly wrong — the residuals, the dashed vertical segments, are long. As the dot descends, the line swings into place and the residuals shorten. Near the end the dot barely moves and the line barely changes: that is convergence, visible.

Point out the dashed path on the surface — that is the trajectory of the run, every iteration recorded. It is steep and fast at the start, slow and short near the bottom, exactly as slide 38 predicted, because the gradient itself shrinks.

If the projector allows, open the original animated GIF full-screen from the resources folder and run it twice. Students remember the motion. Note the axes are labelled w and b rather than θ1 and θ0 — worth saying out loud, since weight and bias are the names used throughout deep learning and they will meet them again in Week 12. Same two numbers, different letters.

The hypothesis, extended

one feature — what we had

hθ(x) = θ0 + θ1x

n features — multivariate linear regression

hθ(x) = θ0 + θ1x1 + θ2x2 + θ3x3 + ⋯ + θnxn

One parameter per feature, plus θ0. Each θj says how much feature j moves the prediction, holding the others fixed.

For the housing example: hθ(x) = θ0 + θ1(size) + θ2(bedrooms) + θ3(floors) + θ4(age).

Speaker notes

Read the housing version in the note aloud, in words: “the predicted price is a base amount, plus so much per square foot, plus so much per bedroom, plus so much per floor, minus so much per year of age.” Said that way, nobody finds it intimidating — it is the estimate a human appraiser would sketch.

Interpretation is the thing to stress, with its caveat. θ1 is dollars per square foot holding bedrooms, floors and age constant. That "holding constant" is doing a lot of work and it is where naive interpretation goes wrong: size and bedrooms are correlated in reality, so you cannot actually vary one alone. The parameters are still useful, but they are not clean causal effects. Say this — it is the single most over-claimed thing about linear models.

Geometry, briefly: with one feature we fit a line in 2-D. With two, a plane in 3-D. With n, a hyperplane in n+1 dimensions. Say "hyperplane" once so the word is not startling later, and do not try to draw it.

Count the parameters: n features means n+1 parameters. Lab 1's dataset would need 31.
MULTIPLE56/65

A trick: define x0 = 1

θ0 is the odd one out — it has no x beside it. So invent one, and set it to 1.

hθ(x) = θ0x0 + θ1x1 + ⋯ + θnxn  with  x0 = 1

Now every term has the same form, so the whole thing is one dot product: hθ(x) = θTx

Speaker notes

Students find this suspicious the first time — “can you just make up a feature?” Yes, and here is why it is legitimate: multiplying θ0 by 1 changes nothing. It is pure notation, bought for free, and it removes an irregularity.

Why it is worth doing: without it, the sum has a special first term that must be handled separately in every formula and every loop. With it, all n+1 terms are identical in form, so the sum collapses to a dot product and the code becomes one line.

Make the NumPy connection concrete, because the lab depends on it: in practice you prepend a column of ones to your feature matrix X, and then X @ theta computes every prediction for every example at once. No Python loop at all. That is orders of magnitude faster and it is how every real implementation does it.

Vocabulary: θ0 is the bias or intercept term. The ones column is sometimes called the bias column. In scikit-learn, fit_intercept=True does this for you silently — worth knowing so the parameter is not mysterious when they meet it in Week 3.

Say the shapes out loud: both x and θ live in ℝn+1, so θTx is a single number. Shape errors are the most common NumPy bug they will hit.

The same rule, written out

One line per parameter. The only difference between them is which feature multiplies the error: θj's update is weighted by xj.

And because x0 = 1, θ0's update has no feature weighting at all — which is exactly the θ0 rule from slide 48. The old case was never special; it was this case with n = 1.

Speaker notes

The closing argument of the section, and a satisfying one: the single-variable rules from slide 48 are not a separate result that we later generalised. They were always the n = 1 instance of this.

Check the claim with them out loud. Set j = 0: the weighting factor is x0(i), which is 1, so it disappears — leaving exactly the θ0 rule. Set j = 1: the factor is x1(i), the θ1 rule. Nothing was bolted on.

That kind of consistency check is a habit worth teaching for its own sake: “when you generalise a formula, always put the old case back in and confirm you recover it. If you don't, you have made an error.”

Then close the section by returning to the gradient-weighting point from slide 47, because it is now visible at scale: if size runs into the thousands and bedrooms runs from 1 to 5, their gradients differ by three orders of magnitude, so θ1 and θ2 move at wildly different speeds and convergence crawls. That is why you scale features before running gradient descent — the StandardScaler step from Lab 1 part 2, now fully explained rather than asserted.

NEXT60/65

The whole lecture

  • The four notionsDataset · model and parameters · cost function · learning algorithm
  • Hypothesishθ(x) = θTx — a line, a plane, a hyperplane
  • Cost functionMean squared error, J(θ) = 12m∑(hθ(x(i)) − y(i))2
  • AlgorithmGradient descent: θj := θj − α ∂J/∂θj, simultaneously for all j
  • Learning rate αA hyperparameter. Too small is slow; too large diverges. Plot J to check.
  • Why it always worksSquared error on a linear model is convex — one bowl, one minimum
  • Data space vs parameter spaceOne dot on the cost surface is one whole line through the data

Speaker notes

Read down the list and ask, at each row, for a one-sentence explanation from a different student. It is a fast, low-stakes check of what actually landed.

If you have to pick one row to test on, pick the last. Data space versus parameter space is the idea that separates students who can reason about optimisation from students who can only recite an update rule — and it is the one that transfers furthest.

Mention that this table is the honest scope of what is examinable from this lecture.

Speaker notes

The purpose of this slide is to stop students filing linear regression away as "the easy week".

Say it directly: “You will not use linear regression much in your careers. You will use everything you learned today, constantly. This was never really a lecture about fitting lines.”

Row 2 is the one to dwell on if you have thirty seconds: backpropagation is not a different algorithm from gradient descent — it is an efficient way of computing the derivatives that gradient descent needs, when the model is a deep composition of functions. Students who arrive at Week 12 believing backprop is something new struggle unnecessarily.

Lab 2 — Data collection and understanding

Before you can fit a line to data, you have to have data — and know whether you can trust it.

  • Where data comes from
  • CSV · Excel · JSON · SQL · API · web
  • Structured vs unstructured
  • NumPy arrays and DataFrames
  • Inspecting a new dataset
  • Basic statistics
You will read real data from five different sources and formats, then describe it with basic statistics. In Lab 3 you fit today's model to it — first by hand with NumPy, then with scikit-learn — and check that the two agree.

Speaker notes

Connect back to the Lab 1 lifecycle explicitly: this is Stage 2 and Stage 3, done properly on data that was not handed to them pre-cleaned by scikit-learn.

Set the expectation that the data will be difficult, and that this is the point: missing values, inconsistent units, duplicated rows, a date column stored as text. “Every hour a professional spends on machine learning, most of it looks like this lab, not like today's lecture.”

The NumPy portion is deliberately aimed at today's material — vectors, broadcasting, the dot product, and building X with its column of ones. Tell them that explicitly so it does not feel like a detour.

The data card is the graduate-level deliverable: provenance, licence, sampling frame, known quality problems. Say why it matters — a model is only as defensible as the account you can give of its data, and in Week 8 they will be asked to defend one.

The Try item is the good one — it takes five minutes and rewards actual thinking. The symmetry holds because the parabola is centred at θ1 = 1, so θ1 = 0 and θ1 = 2 are equidistant from the minimum. Students who see that have understood the shape of J rather than memorised a formula.

The Think item quietly starts project scoping, which is Week 6. Naming the target variable is the single decision most student projects get wrong, and asking for it now, cheaply, saves a lot of rescue work later.

NEXT64/65

One question to leave with

  • We chose squared error because it is smooth, convex and standard.
  • But it punishes one huge mistake far more than many small ones.
  • When would that be exactly what you want — and when would it be dangerous?

Speaker notes

A closing question with no single right answer, which is the point.

Cases where punishing large errors hard is right: structural load estimation, drug dosing, aircraft fuel calculations — anywhere one catastrophic error is worse than many small inconveniences.

Cases where it is dangerous: when your data has outliers that are recording errors rather than real events. Squared error will contort the whole model to accommodate one mistyped house price. MAE, or Huber loss, would shrug it off. Also worth raising: if the outliers belong to a minority group in the data, the choice of loss has fairness consequences — the model will be dragged toward whichever cases produce the biggest squared errors.

Land the general lesson: choosing a loss function is not a mathematical convenience, it is a statement about what kind of mistake you can live with. That is a Stage 1 decision, it belongs to the human, and it is exactly the thinking their Lab 1 reflection asked for.

If time allows, take two or three answers from the room. It makes a better ending than a summary.

Speaker notes

Leave real time. After a mathematical lecture the questions are usually of two kinds, and both deserve answers:

Confidence questions — “do I need to know the calculus for the exam?” Answer honestly and specifically now, because the uncertainty is more damaging than either answer.

Genuine confusions — usually slide 26 (data space vs parameter space) or slide 41 (simultaneous update). If two or more students raise the same one, re-teach it on the board rather than repeating the slide; a second explanation in different words is worth more than a louder version of the first.

If nobody asks anything, ask them: “what was the least clear thing today?” It almost always gets an answer, and it is more useful than silence.
